title: Arthritis Medicines and Supplements: Interaction Checks
meta_title: Do Supplements Interact With Arthritis Medicines? (UK)
meta_description: Check supplements with arthritis medicines: methotrexate, folic acid, biologics and bought painkillers. What to show your pharmacist and when to get help.

content:
Quick answer: Check the exact supplement with a pharmacist or your rheumatology team before taking it with arthritis medicines. Some combinations have known risks; many herbal combinations have not been studied well enough to call safe. Bring the ingredients, strength and a full medicines list. Do not change prescribed treatment or folic acid to make room for a supplement.

This guide is for adults preparing a medicines conversation, not a tool that can clear a combination as safe. A product sold without a prescription can still matter to your treatment. Equally, a possible interaction does not mean everyone taking the combination will be harmed. The medicine, product, dose, kidney and liver health, and other treatments all affect the assessment.

Start with the product, not the promise

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service (SPS) explains that evidence about complementary-product interactions is limited and often based on theory or case reports. Products with similar names can contain different ingredients. A front-of-pack claim such as "joint support" or "immune support" does not establish safety with a prescribed medicine.

Take the packet or clear photographs of the full label to the pharmacist. Include powders, drops, teas, vitamins, minerals and products bought online. Explain why you want to try it and what symptom you hope to improve. If pain or fatigue is not controlled, that also deserves a review of your existing care rather than an assumption that you need another product.

Methotrexate: check folic acid and bought painkillers

NHS methotrexate advice says there is not enough information to establish the safety of other herbal remedies and supplements with methotrexate. If you already have prescribed folic acid, do not add a vitamin or mineral product containing folic acid or folate without advice. Check combination supplements as well as single-vitamin tablets.

Prescribed folic acid is used to reduce methotrexate side effects. Follow your own prescribed dose and day; do not stop it because you have read that vitamins interact. SPS describes several folic-acid regimens and notes that it is usually avoided on the methotrexate day. This is not a reason to claim that any extra dose automatically cancels the treatment. Ask your team if your instructions are unclear or you have made a mistake.

SPS guidance on low-dose methotrexate says it is cleared mainly by the kidneys. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can increase kidney and methotrexate toxicity risks. A specialist may prescribe an NSAID with monitoring, but do not buy an oral NSAID, or a cold remedy containing one, without discussing it with a pharmacist or doctor. Do not stop an existing specialist-prescribed combination on the basis of this page.

Tell every prescriber that you take methotrexate, including when you need antibiotics. SPS advises avoiding trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole with methotrexate because of severe bone-marrow suppression risk. Let the prescriber or pharmacist choose and check treatment; this article does not provide an alternative antibiotic plan.

Sulfasalazine and biologic medicines need individual checks too

The NHS sulfasalazine guide also says that herbal-remedy safety is not established. Sulfasalazine can reduce folic-acid absorption, and the right advice depends on why folic acid is needed. Ask about the actual supplement rather than applying a blanket two-hour spacing rule to all multivitamins or arthritis medicines.

For biologics, check your particular medicine. For example, NHS adalimumab information asks you to tell your doctor or care team about herbal remedies, vitamins and supplements. It also explains the infection risk and precautions with live vaccines. A supplement marketed as an "immune booster" is not a substitute for that advice. This page does not establish that such a product cancels a biologic or inevitably causes a flare.

Turmeric, curcumin and bleeding or liver concerns

Cooking with a spice and taking a concentrated extract are different exposures. The UK Committee on Toxicity assessment describes rare, unpredictable liver injury associated with turmeric supplements, including cases below a dietary intake limit. A label's suggested amount is not a personal guarantee of safety.

Welsh Medicines Advice Service advises caution with medicinal turmeric or curcumin alongside medicines with significant side effects, and with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines because bleeding risk might increase. Much of the interaction evidence is laboratory or animal evidence and may not translate directly to people. Do not turn a theoretical mechanism into a proven interaction rate. See our separate turmeric and methotrexate guide for that specific question.

Check painkillers, cold remedies and other non-prescription products

Supplements are only part of the review. The NHS ibuprofen guide warns against taking ibuprofen at the same time as another NSAID such as naproxen or aspirin because serious side effects can increase. If aspirin has been prescribed for another reason, ask a pharmacist before adding ibuprofen; do not stop the aspirin yourself.

Show the active ingredients in combination cold-and-flu remedies and other painkillers, not only the brand names. Ask the pharmacist to check for duplication and for interactions with every medicine you take. Do not apply a universal spacing interval or a supplement "washout" schedule from an internet article. Before surgery, tell the pre-assessment team about all products early and follow its stopping and restarting instructions.

A checklist for your pharmacist or rheumatology team

  1. What do I take? Bring prescribed medicines, occasional painkillers and every supplement, with the amount and frequency.
  2. What is in this product? Show all ingredients and added absorption enhancers, not just the headline herb.
  3. What changes my risk? Mention kidney or liver problems, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and any planned procedure.
  4. What is known and what is uncertain? Ask whether advice comes from human evidence, a case report or a theoretical concern.
  5. What should I do next? Ask whether to avoid the product, whether monitoring is needed, and which symptoms should prompt urgent advice. Keep a note of the agreed plan.

You can use our blank symptom and medication tracker to organise questions. Do not upload private medicine lists to a public website comment. This guide does not rank supplements or prescribe an effective dose.

When to get help rather than wait for a review

While taking methotrexate, the NHS advises contacting your doctor or NHS 111 immediately for yellow eyes or skin, unexplained bruising or bleeding, signs of infection such as a high temperature or sore throat, or a persistent cough or breathing problems. Mouth ulcers can also be a methotrexate toxicity warning in SPS guidance. Do not wait for a routine blood test or assume a supplement explains the symptom.

Call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as sudden swelling of the mouth or throat with difficulty breathing. If you think you have taken too much of a medicine, get urgent advice rather than using this page to decide whether the amount was safe. Bring the packaging and tell the service what you took and when.
